slides.0.title: Industry, markets and trade
slides.0.subtitle: Shipments, stocks, groups and the supply–demand mechanism
slides.1.title: Shipments and revenue: three years of decline
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Shipments 2023 → 2024 → 2025
slides.1.highlights.0.content: About 299 million bottles in 2023 (backed out from the −9.2% in 2024); 271.4 million in 2024, down 9.2%; about 266 million in 2025, down roughly 2% (Comité Champagne, Vinetur). Figures are revised each year, so every number here carries its year
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Domestic versus export
slides.1.highlights.1.content: 2024: France 118.2 million (−7.2%), export 153.2 million (−10.8%), exports 56.4% of the total. 2025: France about 114 million and export about 152 million, exports about 57% (our calculation); more than 80% of the 2025 decline came from the French market (Vinetur). Takeaway: exports are the majority, but recent pressure has mostly come from France
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Revenue
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Industry figures quoted by Vinetur: about €6.3 billion in 2022 (the peak), €6.2 billion in 2023, €5.8 billion in 2024 and a provisional €5.7 billion in 2025 (−1.7%). The official site did not give full-year 2025 revenue in this review, so this is a provisional second-hand figure. Volume fell faster than value, implying a higher average price or a shift to higher price tiers
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Why the decline?
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Causes compiled by Vinetur: shipments pulled forward before US tariffs left distributors overstocked, weak French demand and political uncertainty, inflation and geopolitical tension damping celebratory spending, and a strong euro making Champagne dearer for sterling, dollar and yen buyers. These are industry explanations, not a single cause; imports to the UK, Japan and Canada still grew in 2025
slides.1.content: Mind the vintages of the data: Comité Champagne Key Figures exist in 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions. Every number here is dated; for the exam learn the direction: three falling years, exports above half, recent pressure concentrated in France.
slides.2.title: Stock, reserve and the marketable yield
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Stock in the cellars
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Real Review (2025): houses’ stock stood at about 1,523 million bottles at the end of July 2024, excluding reserves, which it equates with more than five years of sales; houses aim for about 3.5 years and the CIVC states 3.8. Other sources often say “about four years”. The gap comes from definitions (reserves included or not, which year’s sales), so it is flagged here and kept out of the quiz
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Reserve is an extra buffer
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The Real Review estimates reserves could add about 257 million bottles (July 2024) and says the reserve cap is “usually 8,000 kg/ha”, which differs from the INAO specification’s 10,000 kg/ha (flagged in Level 2; the specification prevails). The point: stock plus reserve lets Champagne ride out successive small harvests and also makes oversupply pressure greater
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The marketable yield is cut year by year
slides.2.highlights.2.content: 11,400 kg/ha in 2023, 10,000 in 2024 and 9,000 in 2025 (Journal du Luxe; the 2025 limit equates to about 255 million bottles per The Real Review). The Comité’s stated reasons: match supply to demand, protect value, avoid downward price pressure, with economic and geopolitical instability and more volatile consumer behaviour cited (Comité Champagne, Journal du Luxe). It is supply management, not a quality decision
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Where does the excess go?
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Output above the marketable yield may go into reserve under the rules; The Real Review estimated the 2025 crop at about 13,000–14,000 kg/ha, with the excess over 9,000 able to go into reserve. In other words the marketable yield limits what can be sold this year, not how much the vines can bear (the structural ceilings remain 12,400 and 15,500; Level 2)
slides.2.content: Link the three mechanisms: marketable yield (this year) → reserve (across years) → stock (finished wine). MW questions often ask how together they stabilise price.
slides.3.title: Group structure and the producer landscape
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Big groups: LVMH and Pernod Ricard
slides.3.highlights.0.content: LVMH’s Moët Hennessy owns six Champagne brands (including Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Dom Pérignon, Ruinart, Krug and Mercier). Pernod Ricard owns G.H. Mumm and Perrier-Jouët; from February 2025 media reported that it was weighing a sale of Mumm (a report, not a conclusion; not examined)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Mid-sized groups and recent deals
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Piper-Heidsieck and Charles Heidsieck: sold by Rémy Cointreau to EPI in 2015 (Decanter). Lanson-BCC: in October 2025 it agreed to buy 100% of Heidsieck & Co. Monopole for €50 million, effective 1 January 2026, with vintage and packaged stock priced separately; the brand shipped 2.7 million bottles in 2024 (IWSR; about four in five exported) (The Drinks Business). The deal replaced an earlier arrangement under which Compagnie Vranken was to acquire it. The source does not name the seller, so none is given here
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Market structure (single source, flagged)
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The Real Review (2025): growers own 88% of vineyards; about 66% of grapes harvested by growers are sold to the large houses (and rising); the largest 100 houses account for over two-thirds of volume and 85% of exports; the six largest groups took 75% of 2024 turnover; LVMH has about 18% of volume and 22% of value; grower labels together hold 18% of volume and 15% of value. Note that Decanter (2023) puts Moët Hennessy at about 30% of worldwide Champagne sales by value, against 22% here — sources and definitions differ, so none of this is examined
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The structural tension between growers and houses
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Growers sell grapes by the kilo and tend to want high yields; houses sell wine and fear oversupply pushing down prices (Academie du Vin, Level 2). The Comité Champagne, jointly made up of the SGV and the UMC, institutionalises that tension. Grape prices per kilo are negotiated within the industry; no verifiable current figure was obtained in this review, so none is given
slides.3.content: Company and personal facts are included only where a source supports them: sellers, shareholdings and personnel that could not be verified are left out.
slides.4.title: MW essay material: yield limits and brands
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The prompt: does supply management work?
slides.4.highlights.0.content: For: limiting marketable yield and using reserves stabilise price and brand value, so revenue has fallen less than volume (2025: volume about −2%, value about −1.7%; 2024: volume −9.2%, value about −6.5%, the latter derived here from €5.8 and €6.2 billion). Against: stocks stay high, growers’ income is constrained, and consumers face price-elasticity risk when prices rise
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Brand versus place
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The big groups manage Champagne as brand and luxury (high prices, global distribution), while grower labels express village and vintage. Champagne is unusual in having both a strong brand and a strong place name: the AOC protects the place, companies build the brands, and each amplifies the other
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Indicators of price and value
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Useful indicators: shipments against revenue, export share, domestic–export split, stock-to-sales ratio, the gap between marketable yield and actual crop, price-tier mix. When quoting, give year and source and state the basis (reserves included or not, provisional or final)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Risks and external shocks
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Tariffs and exchange rates (US front-loading that overstocked distributors, a strong euro), weak French demand, climate-driven crop swings, generational change and the low-alcohol trend; tie each back to “is supply management still enough?”. Only modest growth is hoped for in 2026 (Vinetur, quoting industry figures); this lesson makes no forecast
slides.4.content: This page is a materials bank: ch-l3-6 shows how to turn it into an argued essay.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Who decides the yearly marketable yield?
The Comité Champagne, made up of the SGV and UMC, sets it each summer; the specification also sets structural ceilings of 12,400 and 15,500 (Level 2).
Which statement matches the Comité data for 2024 and 2025?
A. Exports are more than half of shipments (about 56–57%)
B. The French market is more than half
Exports were 56.4% in 2024 and about 57% in 2025; figures update each year, so remember the structure: exports are the majority.
When demand falls, what is the main logic behind the Comité lowering the marketable yield?
A. To raise the wine’s quality tier
B. To reduce the planted area
D. To match supply to demand, protect value and avoid downward price pressure
This is supply management, not a quality decision; excess may go into reserve under the rules (Level 2 and this lesson).
